name: ShotDeck
tagline: A searchable library of movie stills for shot references and lookbooks.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: ShotDeck is not a search app, it is a corpus: hundreds of thousands of film stills tagged by lens, lighting, color, framing, shot size, interior/exterior, era, and more. The software around it is unremarkable, a faceted search UI with lightboxes and PDF export, and an agent could rough that out in a session. What it cannot do is produce the images or the tags, which come from licensed-ish screen grabs and years of human annotation by people who know what a 35mm dutch two-shot looks like. Build your own and you get an empty shelf plus a scraping problem with real copyright teeth. The honest consolation is a personal lookbook tool that indexes stills you grab yourself.
coreLoopDIY: A local faceted image library where you drop your own frame grabs, tag them by shot size, lens, lighting and color, then filter and export a lookbook PDF.
requirements: Your own collection of frame grabs (you supply the images)
Optional: ffmpeg for pulling frames from your own video files
Optional: a vision model API key if you want auto-tagging suggestions
whatYouLose: The actual library: hundreds of thousands of pre-grabbed, pre-tagged stills from real films
Consistent taxonomy applied by people who understand cinematography vocabulary
Attribution metadata: film, year, DP, director, camera and lens where known
Discovery by browsing, finding the reference you did not know you wanted
Any legal cover for redistributing frames from commercial films
moatNotes: The taxonomy is as valuable as the images. Tagging a still correctly for lens length and lighting direction is a skilled judgment call, not a checkbox.
whyPeopleStillPay: Directors, DPs and ad agencies pay because a lookbook is due tomorrow and they need twenty shots that all say the same thing about warm practical light in a moving car. Searching a curated, correctly tagged corpus takes minutes. Assembling the same references from memory, Google Images and your own screenshot folder takes an afternoon and produces worse results. The subscription is cheaper than the hour it saves per project, and nobody on a production wants to be the person who built a tool instead of finding the shot.
notes: The search UI is a weekend build; the archive is not. The moat is a quarter million frame grabs with cinematography-literate tags and the rights posture to host them.
prompt:
Build a local-first visual reference library for film stills called "Frames". Personal use, single user, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Next.js with the App Router, TypeScript, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Tailwind for styling. Images live on disk in ./library/images, thumbnails in ./library/thumbs. Everything runs with `npm run dev` on localhost.

Core features:
1. Ingest: a watched folder ./inbox. A script `npm run ingest` moves any jpg/png/webp into ./library/images, generates a 480px-wide thumbnail with sharp, computes a perceptual hash to skip duplicates, extracts the dominant 5-color palette, and inserts a row into SQLite.
2. Frame extraction: `npm run grab -- path/to/video.mp4 --every 10s` shells out to ffmpeg and dumps frames into ./inbox. Fail with a clear message if ffmpeg is not on PATH.
3. Tagging UI: a grid view of all stills. Click one to open a detail panel with editable fields: title, film, year, director, cinematographer, and multi-select facets for shot size (extreme wide, wide, medium, medium close, close, extreme close), angle (eye level, high, low, dutch, overhead), lens feel (wide, normal, long, anamorphic), lighting (hard, soft, high key, low key, practical, silhouette, natural), time of day, interior/exterior, and free-form tags. Keyboard shortcuts: arrow keys to move, number keys to apply the last-used facet, `f` to favorite.
4. Search: left sidebar of facet checkboxes plus a text box that matches title, film, people and tags. Filters combine as AND across facet groups and OR within a group. Also allow color search: pick a swatch, rank results by distance to their dominant palette.
5. Boards: create named boards, drag stills onto them, reorder, then export a board as a PDF contact sheet (3 per page, caption under each) using pdf-lib.

Explicitly out of scope: no scraping, no downloading images from any third party, no bundled dataset. The library starts empty and the user fills it with their own material. Do not add an image search API.

Optional and off by default: if OPENAI_API_KEY is present in .env, add a "suggest tags" button on the detail panel that sends the thumbnail to a vision model and pre-fills the facet fields for human confirmation. Never auto-apply. Read secrets only from .env, and commit a .env.example.

Deliver a README with setup, the three npm scripts, and a note that the SQLite file plus the library folder is the entire backup.
